name: Hypoxia preconditioned plasma

card.summary: An experimental blood-derived plasma, made by incubating a person's own blood under low oxygen so cells release growth factors, studied as a possible next-generation alternative to platelet-rich plasma for skin and tissue regeneration.
card.note: Studied mainly in lab and animal wound-healing work; not an established cosmetic treatment.

quick.overview:
Hypoxia preconditioned plasma (HPP) is plasma obtained after a person's own blood has been kept under low-oxygen conditions outside the body, which prompts blood cells to release growth factors in response to a wound-like environment. Researchers have proposed it as an autologous alternative to platelet-rich plasma (PRP).

Its link to appearance is the same one made for PRP: growth factors that support new blood vessels and collagen could aid skin and tissue repair. Published work so far is mostly in vitro and animal wound-healing research, and a 2025 study reported faster diabetic wound closure in animals.
quick.how: In the research literature, anticoagulated blood is cultured under hypoxic conditions at body temperature and the plasma is collected for use, for example in gels. Nothing in the sources describes it as a routine cosmetic service.
quick.risks: Human safety data are not described in the cited work. Related PRP treatments are generally reported as having low adverse-event rates in trials, with infection risk linked to unsterile practice rather than the plasma itself.

lead: Hypoxia preconditioned plasma is made by culturing a person's anticoagulated blood under low oxygen and body temperature so the cells release angiogenic growth factors; the plasma is then separated and used [1]. It was proposed in 2014 as a next-generation autologous therapy compared with currently available blood-based products such as PRP [1].

For looks, the idea is regenerative: growth factors such as VEGF, PDGF and EGF promote new blood vessels and collagen, which could support skin and wound repair [2]. In standard PRP, platelets are concentrated and injected for facial rejuvenation and hair, a context in which HPP is positioned as an alternative [3].
Published studies are laboratory and animal work, including comparisons with PRP in vitro and a mouse study of a serum-hydrogel [4][5].

chain: Blood cultured under low oxygen releases growth factors
Possible faster repair and collagen deposition
angle.text: Researchers propose HPP as a growth-factor-rich autologous preparation for wounds and tissue regeneration. Cosmetic use is an extrapolation from PRP-style treatments.

paras: HPP exposes peripheral blood cells to hypoxic stress outside the body. The resulting plasma is enriched in angiogenic factors and is meant to mimic the response of blood cells to a wound [1].

A 2025 Scientific Reports study found that HPP contained significantly more VEGF, PDGF, EGF, IGF, TSP1 and PF4, promoted cell proliferation, migration and tube formation in vitro, and accelerated wound closure in diabetic animals (84 percent versus 65 percent) [2]. Earlier in vitro work compared hypoxia-preconditioned blood-derived secretomes with PRP on angiogenic potential [4], and a mouse pilot study tested a hypoxia-preconditioned serum hydrogel on dermal wounds [5].
No studies found in humans. Related laboratory and animal studies are described above.

timeline.event: Autologous hypoxia preconditioned plasma described in Organogenesis [1].
In vitro comparison with PRP published [4].
Diabetic wound-healing study in Scientific Reports [2].
